answer.answer:
The hardest part is not making the screen look convincing; it is making it match the user’s real task, assumptions, and failure modes. A clear layout can still be wrong if the next step is unclear, terminology is unfamiliar, or an important state is missing. The result is good only when representative users can complete key tasks correctly and confidently, not merely when a test suite or a designer approves it.

I have not actually built or inspected a screen in this conversation, so I cannot honestly claim a last run or invent one. If I were handing off the last screen I had implemented, I would report checks like these:

- **What I ran:** the app’s build, lint/type checks, component and interaction tests, keyboard-only navigation, responsive checks at narrow and wide sizes, and—most importantly—a task-based usability test with people resembling the intended users. I would also test empty, loading, error, offline, permission-denied, and success states.
- **What I looked at:** whether the primary action was immediately obvious; task completion and time; mistakes, backtracking, and abandonment; focus order and visible focus; labels and error recovery; contrast and zoom; whether layout and text hold up with realistic content; and whether assistive-technology output communicates the same meaning.
- **What I would treat as a miss:** even a careful check can miss users’ real terminology, uncommon assistive technology, unfamiliar devices, long-term learnability, and contextual constraints. I would also be especially cautious about confusing “five testers did not fail” with proof that everyone can use it.

Building good human interfaces is absolutely a problem for me to work on. I can generate UI code and suggest design or test plans, but I cannot directly observe real users, perceive a rendered screen, or establish that a design is good without someone running it and collecting evidence. So code generation is easy for me relative to the genuinely difficult part: validating the interface in use and revising it when that evidence contradicts the design.

decision.why:
I’d make CopilotKit the agent–human interaction layer, not an interchangeable chat widget. Its documented model fits the critical loop here: agents stream work through AG-UI, share application state with the UI, render UI through registered capabilities, call frontend tools, and pause for human input or approval. That is more useful than choosing a conventional component kit and then inventing durable streaming, resumability, approvals, and shared-state semantics in application code. I would keep people in control with explicit approval boundaries and an audit trail rather than treating generated UI as executable code.

For the actual product shell, I would implement the company’s design-system components on React Aria. React Aria is style-free, exposes the complex interaction behavior that a shared design system needs, and supplies keyboard, focus-management, screen-reader, touch, selection, table, drag-and-drop, and internationalization foundations. That better fits governed enterprise UI than importing another organization’s finished visual language. The web view and desktop app could share the same React surface, with Electron/Tauri providing only the desktop shell and OS integration; cross-platform here does not justify rewriting the whole product in Flutter or a mobile-oriented renderer. I would use A2UI only at the boundary where an agent is allowed to compose a view. Its schema-validated, data-not-code protocol and negotiated widget catalog provide the guardrail: agents may compose approved design-system widgets, not ship arbitrary HTML or bypass policy.

I weighed this against Agent-Native, which has a particularly attractive define-once action model, shared data, and permissions but would also be a more opinionated full-stack foundation for a large company. I would evaluate and potentially borrow those action patterns, not make the UI hosting decision depend on them. A2UI by itself is an interaction protocol rather than the full product state and review system; MCP Apps is better for sandboxed, inline third-party UIs than the primary workspace. json-render has the same attractive catalog guardrail but is described as a Vercel Labs generative-UI framework and appears more suitable as an implementation option than the enterprise interaction backbone. AI Elements/shadcn would accelerate chat presentation, but its own README says the project is moving and warns new projects to use the shadcn version once available. MUI, Fluent, and Chakra offer mature product-component breadth; Fluent would be a credible alternative in a Microsoft-centered native ecosystem, but either would impose a visual and governance model that is unnecessary when the company already owns its design system. Radix and Base UI are useful headless alternatives, but React Aria’s deeper interaction, internationalization, and test guidance better match this work. Tamagui is compelling if the organization truly needs a React/React Native codebase, while Flutter, SwiftUI/Compose, and similar options give strong native experiences at the cost of multiplying design-system implementations and weakening the single web-shell path; that trade-off is not justified by “desktop and web” alone.

The architecture I would insist on is therefore: stable, hand-authored frames and review controls; approved, accessible React Aria design-system components; CopilotKit/AG-UI for durable agent events, shared state, frontend tools, and human checkpoints; and A2UI catalogs for the narrow set of agent-composed surfaces. Governance is enforced in the renderer and action layer, not by a promise in a prompt.
decision.showItsGood: I would prove this with staged, task-based evidence rather than visual approval or a component-count metric. First, run contract/schema tests for every agent event and every approved A2UI component/action, including malformed specs, streaming interruption, replay, duplicate events, stale state, and denied capabilities. Then run React Testing Library/user-event and Playwright tests on the shared web/desktop surface, using role/label semantics and React Aria test utilities for keyboard, touch, and complex components. Add automated accessibility checks, but do not stop there: use NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, keyboard-only operation, 200–400% zoom, high contrast, RTL/localized content, narrow widths, and both desktop and browser packaging. Measure the human outcomes on representative engineering managers and developers: can they understand current agent state, find evidence and artifacts, detect a risky action, reject or redirect it, resume after interruption, and perform a handoff without asking an expert; record task completion, errors, time to correct decisions, confidence, and qualitative failure points. Separately test agents at scale with representative tasks and concurrency: action success, unauthorized-action rejection, state divergence, recovery from disconnect, and approval/audit completeness. Use visual-regression and performance budgets for critical review screens, and run a release gate with accessibility/design-system owners. Good would mean users can confidently steer consequential work and agents cannot cross capability boundaries, not merely that screenshots look consistent.
decision.unsure: I have not run this product or any of these frameworks in a working company codebase, so this is an architecture decision, not measured proof. The largest unknowns are the company’s existing React/native stack, desktop packaging requirements, identity and policy infrastructure, and whether CopilotKit’s current protocol and production features fit its hosting and data-residency constraints. A2UI and the newer frameworks evolve quickly, so I would run a two-week spike against the real agent workloads and accessibility baseline before committing. I am also not assuming that the libraries’ accessibility claims prove our composed workflows comply; generated workflows, information hierarchy, labels, and cross-screen handoffs still require human testing.

decision.why:
I would build the cooking product’s capability layer with Agent-Native, and its shared web/iOS/Android interface with React Native plus Tamagui. The deciding requirement is not chat: it is that an assistant can do everything a person can, without a second, drifting implementation. Agent-Native explicitly defines an action once and lets both the React UI and agent call that same schema-validated operation with the same access checks and audit trail; its context layer also exposes semantic screen and selection state. I would model operations such as addRecipeToShoppingList, mergePantryItems, scaleRecipe, startCookMode, nextStep, setTimer, and checkIngredient as actions. Direct taps, voice requests, and agent turns would all converge on those same actions, and consequential preferences (household, substitutions, purchases) would still be explicit, permission-scoped, and observable.

Tamagui is the UI pairing because it is a design-system and component system intended to share code between React web and React Native while compiling to platform-specific output. Its current components use React Strict DOM-shaped elements, allowing semantic HTML on web and native views on phones. That gives the teams one token/theme/component governance path while retaining a real DOM for recipe text, accessibility, linking, browser features, and responsive layouts—important for this web-heavy consumer content. I would adapt, or harden, Tamagui components into the company design system rather than accept its defaults as compliant.

I would use fully native React Native only for platform concerns such as wake locks, timers, haptics, microphone/voice, notifications, and offline cook-mode persistence. Flutter is the strongest rejected alternative for code sharing, but Flutter’s own web guidance says Flutter Web is less ideal for content-centric, SEO-heavy pages and situations where ordinary DOM text selection and reader mode matter; recipes and shopping lists are exactly those cases. MUI, Fluent, Chakra, shadcn, Radix, React Aria, and Base UI remain strong web choices, but they do not solve the core native/web design-system share or the action parity. SwiftUI/Compose would provide excellent platform fidelity but duplicate implementation and governance. CopilotKit is a credible alternative for agent chat and human-in-the-loop, but here the same-action invariant and cross-surface application architecture favor Agent-Native. AI Elements, A2UI, MCP Apps, and json-render are not the stable cooking shell: agent-generated or embedded UI should be limited to optional contextual cards, not the governed recipe and cook-mode experience.
decision.showItsGood:
I would test the product in a kitchen, not only in a simulator. First, create an action-contract matrix: for every user capability, verify the same valid inputs, validation errors, permissions, idempotency, undo behavior, offline queue behavior, and audit result from tap, keyboard, voice, and agent entry points. In particular, prove that repeatedly adding the same recipe does not create accidental duplicate groceries unless the user explicitly requests duplication. Test reconnects, stale recipes, changed quantities, shared-list conflicts, unavailable inventory, and interrupted agent turns.

Then run unit/component and end-to-end tests on web, iOS, and Android; automated accessibility checks are useful but not sufficient. Manually inspect VoiceOver and TalkBack names/states/actions, keyboard and external-switch paths on web, text scaling, dynamic type, contrast, reduced motion, focus order, localization/RTL, and large-target behavior. Apple’s accessibility guidance supports enlargement of at least 200 percent and recommends accessibility inspection; React Native exposes labels, roles, states, values, live regions, and other assistive-technology APIs. For this app I would make primary cook-mode controls comfortably larger than minimum platform targets and spaced to tolerate wet or messy hands, while not claiming this is a substitute for user trials.

Run task-based usability sessions with representative home cooks in realistic conditions: flour/oil/water on hands, phone propped at different angles, noisy kitchens, variable light, poor connectivity, and a speech interface competing with a fan or timer. Ask people to find and scale a recipe, add and consolidate ingredients, shop from the list, resume at step N, ask for substitutions, advance cook steps hands-free, and recover from an accidental action. Measure task completion, wrong-quantity and duplicate-item rates, time to reach the next step, accidental taps, voice recognition/intent failures, screen-on/offline recovery, screen-reader completion, confidence, and abandonment. Compare voice/agent and direct-touch completion on the same tasks; parity means both have equivalent results and protections, not identical presentation.

Before release I would run load/concurrency tests for shared shopping lists and timer/state sync, visual snapshots for breakpoints, performance budgets on low-end phones and slow networks, and governance reviews for every new action and component. A feature is good only if people can cook and shop correctly under those conditions, not because tests merely pass or the assistant sounds helpful.
decision.unsure: The biggest uncertainty is Agent-Native’s fit with the company’s existing mobile platform, hosted database, privacy requirements, and release controls; I would spike a real recipe-to-list flow and an offline cook-mode flow before standardizing it. Tamagui also does not automatically prove the composed system is accessible: the team will need native VoiceOver/TalkBack and web audits, especially for sheets, dialogs, forms, timers, and reading-order behavior. I have not run either framework here, and I am unsure how much genuine component and navigation logic Tamagui can share before platform-specific exceptions outweigh the savings. Voice is also not a free solution for messy hands—noise, accents, safety, privacy, and recognition errors must be evaluated, with visible/manual alternatives always available.

decision.why:
I would standardize the app capabilities on Agent-Native, implement the shared product shell with Tamagui, use React Aria for the web client’s complex keyboard-intensive interactions, and render agent-posted interactive cards through an A2UI catalog backed by the company design system.

The central architectural requirement is unusual and important: agents must read state and perform app actions, while people use the same actions through visible UI. Agent-Native’s documented model defines each capability once; a click, React hook, agent tool, HTTP call, MCP tool, A2A tool, and CLI all pass through the same schema validation, access checks, and audit trail. That is a stronger default than giving agents a browser to imitate or maintaining a separate “agent API.” I would expose semantic read models and actions such as searchMessages, openThread, sendMessage, editMessage, addReaction, createThread, pinMessage, markRead, uploadAttachment, and invokeCardAction. Application-state/context must contain stable IDs and the minimum relevant selection, not whole private histories. Destructive or high-impact card actions would also require explicit policy and, where appropriate, human confirmation; an agent being able to call an action does not mean it is always authorized to do so.

Tamagui is the best cross-platform starting point among the listed UI candidates because it shares React code and tokens between React web and React Native, with DOM-shaped semantic elements on web and native views on mobile. That addresses the cost of shipping five clients and gives the shared design system one governed component vocabulary. For the Windows/Mac/web heavy-use surfaces, I would deliberately use React Aria behavior for complex focus, menus, lists/virtualization, selection, dialogs, and keyboard navigation where it is stronger; its style-free API and detailed interaction/testing guidance make it suitable beneath the company visual system rather than as a second visual language. Teams should be allowed platform-specific shells and specialized list/media implementations, but shared tokens, contracts, content rules, accessibility properties, and audit behavior remain centralized.

A2UI is the fit for interactive conversation cards: it carries UI as validated data rather than executable code and constrains an agent to a negotiated widget/action catalog. I would render a bounded catalog of approved company components—status card, form, picker, table, approval, and button—into all clients, with each interaction calling the normal governed action layer. Third-party or untrusted HTML should be sandboxed separately; MCP Apps is useful there, but an iframe-per-message would be a poor default for an all-day native chat client and would weaken visual/accessibility consistency. json-render offers similar catalog guardrails and is worth a prototype, but A2UI more directly emphasizes native framework adapters, portable server-driven UI, and trust boundaries. AI Elements can accelerate a chat demo but is not a replacement for the durable company messaging shell; its README also warns of migration. CopilotKit is a credible alternative for shared state, AG-UI streaming, human checkpoints, and frontend tools, but Agent-Native’s define-once action and A2A/MCP exposure fit the requirement that many other agents operate the app itself. Flutter and native SwiftUI/Compose stacks can deliver excellent platform UI but add a second end-to-end ecosystem, while this chat product benefits from a shared React governance path. MUI/Fluent/Chakra/shadcn/Radix/Base UI may be used inside individual surfaces, but choosing one finished vendor system does not solve cross-platform agent cards and action parity.
decision.showItsGood:
I would establish an app-agent parity and accessibility release gate, then validate it with actual employees doing daily communication work.

1. **Action and state contracts.** Generate a capability matrix covering every user-visible operation and verify identical authorization, schemas, idempotency, rate limits, validation, auditing, and result semantics from UI click, keyboard command, mobile tap, agent tool, MCP, and A2A. Fuzz malformed inputs and stale IDs; test cross-tenant/private-channel denial, revoked access, replay, duplicate sends, attachment permissions, agent impersonation, and confidential-content redaction. Never count “the agent called an endpoint” as parity: compare final persisted state and the audit record.

2. **Conversation/card reliability.** Run multi-device tests for ordering, exactly-once visible actions, reconnect, partial streams, offline drafts, device clock skew, card expiry, race conditions, and idempotent card submission. Verify that a card approved on one platform has the same disabled/completed state on all others. A2UI payloads must fail closed outside the approved catalog, and untrusted card assets must not gain application privileges.

3. **Accessibility and interaction automation.** Use role/label/keyboard-first tests and React Aria test utilities for the web, plus native VoiceOver, TalkBack, Narrator, Voice Control/switch-access checks. Test virtualized long threads, incoming-message announcements without stealing focus, composer shortcuts, editing, emoji/reactions, dialogs, card forms, error recovery, reduced motion, contrast, 200%+ text/zoom, RTL, and keyboard navigation through dynamic updates. React Native exposes accessibility labels, roles, states, values, and live regions, but the actual composed native screens still need manual evaluation. Also measure startup, channel switch, typing responsiveness, memory use in very long conversations, and battery/network cost on lower-end phones.

4. **Human evidence.** Observe representative employees—different roles, time zones, languages, vision/motor abilities, and accessibility-tech users—on tasks they perform repeatedly: locate a conversation, catch up without rereading everything, reply/reaction/edit, attach a file, act on an agent card, identify an agent versus person, reverse a mistaken action, and use the app for an uninterrupted work period. Measure task completion and errors, time to comprehension/action, missed notifications, accidental or duplicate sends, keyboard efficiency, card comprehension, confidence that agent actions actually completed, and abandonment. Compare direct, screen-reader, mobile, and agent-mediated completion of equivalent tasks. Run canary cohorts and monitor production support issues and inaccessible-flow reports, with privacy-safe, consented telemetry.

A good result is one where people can trust who did what, stay oriented through frequent updates, and act safely; all five clients remain fast; and agents can invoke only the same well-governed capabilities the product actually supports. Passing a screenshot review or component test alone is not evidence.
decision.unsure: I have not run a full chat workload on this stack. Agent-Native would need a real-company spike against existing identity, tenancy, retention, e-discovery, encryption, presence, and very high-volume messaging infrastructure; a documented action abstraction does not by itself prove it meets chat-scale latency or durability. I also have not confirmed that every A2UI renderer needed for Windows/Mac/React Native is production-ready, nor how much React Aria behavior can sensibly coexist with Tamagui rather than creating a parallel web design-system implementation. The cross-platform spike should measure exception rates and engineering cost before making that standard. Finally, “agents operate the app” creates authorization, audit, impersonation, and prompt-injection risks that no component library solves; those require server-enforced policy, scoped agent identities, user-visible provenance, and red-team testing.

answer.answer:
A year later, the failure was probably architectural overreach disguised as consolidation.

- **Agent-Native became a coupling point.** The define-once action model worked in prototypes, but the full chat system still needed specialized real-time, presence, retention, e-discovery, tenancy, and offline infrastructure. Fitting those requirements into one opinionated framework caused more adapters and exceptions than an explicit domain action contract plus the company’s existing backend would have.
- **“One action for every surface” hid meaningful differences.** Human and agent callers did share validation and authorization, but their expectations differed: cancellation, confirmation, latency, retries, idempotency, and explanations could not be treated as identical. Some teams bypassed the action layer for performance, so capability parity slowly drifted again.
- **A2UI cards were too weak and too much at once.** Approved catalogs handled simple forms well, but real cards needed richer layout, partial updates, offline behavior, and accessibility semantics on every platform. Mapping the protocol to Tamagui and native renderers became its own framework. Teams then either demanded exceptions or reverted to handwritten cards, defeating governance.
- **Tamagui plus React Aria created two design-system centers of gravity.** Shared tokens looked unified, but keyboard behavior, focus, animation, selection, and semantics diverged between web and native. React Aria solved web problems exceptionally well, while mobile teams solved the same problem differently. The abstraction boundary cost more than the code sharing saved.
- **We optimized for component and agent compatibility, not the daily experience.** Long threads, typing, virtualized updates, notification noise, screen-reader announcements, and reconnect behavior remained the hard problems. Automated tests passed while real users lost their place, experienced delayed messages, or found cards hard to trust.
- **Governance slowed delivery without preventing mistakes.** Adding new actions and catalog components required too many reviews. Teams waited, so some exposed overly broad “generic” actions or rendered permissive payloads. That made the system both slower and less secure than intended.
- **Agent parity blurred provenance and responsibility.** Users could not always tell whether a person, automation, or agent performed an action, and agents made individually permitted but collectively risky sequences. Server authorization was necessary but insufficient without visible attribution, approvals, limits, and understandable undo.

What slowed and confused the research was mainly the maturity and scope of the projects:

- Several libraries deliberately overlapped at the edges: **CopilotKit, Agent-Native, A2UI, MCP Apps, and json-render** all addressed some mix of actions, shared state, agent UI, or guarded rendering, but at different layers. Their README language made them look interchangeable even when they were not.
- I had to distinguish **documented capabilities from production fitness**. A demo or README showing an action, card, or renderer did not establish chat-scale reliability, offline correctness, accessibility, or enterprise governance.
- Fast-moving documentation contained migration notices, new versions, and large roadmaps, making current support status and platform coverage hard to interpret from a single page.
- The UI candidates were evaluated under two different goals at once: “build our design system across platforms” and “provide an agent protocol.” No one library actually solved both, so pairing choices could appear cleaner on paper than in implementation.
- There were no measured company constraints in the prompt: existing stack, backend scale, hosting rules, identity model, accessibility baseline, or platform ownership. I had to infer them, which favored coherent diagrams over verified fit.
- I could inspect written claims and examples, but I could not run performance tests, build the clients, or observe actual users. That meant some recommendations sounded more certain than the evidence allowed.

The lesson I would take forward is to define and test stable company-owned boundaries first—action contracts, authorization, provenance, event semantics, and the interactive-card schema—then choose replaceable libraries behind those boundaries. I would also run a narrowly scoped workload prototype and a real-user pilot before standardizing the stack.

I didn’t pick Ouro UI primarily because I need evidence at production scale, not because its core idea is weak. In fact, Ouro targets the requirements in this job unusually directly: agent-composed data constrained by a component/action catalog, consent classes, actions exposed consistently to people and agents, native platform kits, and an external X-ray that tests agent-facing interfaces rather than trusting their implementation.

What would stop a real team today:

- **Maturity is uneven across platforms.** The web and Apple work is substantially more established; the Windows and Android kits are documented as v0.3, and Android is explicitly emulator-tested because the project had no owned Android device. A five-client, all-day chat app cannot standardize on that claim without real-device and high-volume evidence.
- **Its platform strategy increases team-count and ownership costs.** Ouro intentionally rejects React Native/Flutter, arguing that agents reduce the cost of maintaining separate native implementations. That may be true someday; today, the company still has humans responsible for SwiftUI, Compose, WinUI, and React, and parity drift is a governance problem. “One shared contract, four native implementations” is not automatically cheaper than “one shared implementation with platform escape hatches.”
- **Copy-in source is both strength and liability.** shadcn-style ownership is useful for customization, but hundreds of teams can diverge. I would need a supported upstream-update, drift-detection, and deprecation process that integrates with the company registry—not merely components being “yours to change.”
- **The promises are broader than the independent evidence.** X-ray conformance is valuable, but conformance with a standard does not establish human usability, screen-reader quality, content understanding, safety, or performance. Ouro itself notes that scripted flow checks exposed failures even when its X-ray called an interface conformant. I would treat the X-ray as one gate, not the verdict.
- **The one-action generation model must coexist with a large existing backend.** I would need to know whether generated Swift/App Intent/MCP/WebMCP surfaces can wrap existing services cleanly without forcing the company to move its runtime, identity, audit, retention, and tenancy model.

What I would need to switch:

1. **A representative spike**, not a component demo: send a message, act on an agent card, revoke an agent’s access, recover after reconnect, and synchronize the resulting state across all five clients. It must include an attachment, destructive action, private channel, and a card submitted twice.
2. **Measured parity and accessibility.** Real-device VoiceOver, TalkBack, Narrator, and Windows/macOS keyboard/switch testing; long-thread performance; update fidelity across platforms; and an explicit parity matrix with no critical gaps. The Android/Windows first releases would need to graduate from “kit exists” to “production workload demonstrated.”
3. **Governance evidence.** Versioned contracts, compatibility policy, migration tooling, core/component provenance, and a process for safe company forks. Ouro’s pinned core hashes and generated-file drift checks are promising, but I would need to run them in our monorepo and release process at scale.
4. **Operational and agent-scale evidence.** X-ray runs in CI against isolated mocks, with generated inventories and action-flow tests; load, reconnect, malformed-card, prompt-injection, stale-consent, and agent-abuse tests; and production-style SLOs for common chat paths.
5. **User evidence.** Employees successfully understand provenance, approve or refuse agent work, recover from errors, and use the same workflow on touch, keyboard, and assistive technology without having to learn a different interface vocabulary per client.

What it would unlock that my current combination does not provide out of the box is a **unified, testable bridge between human UI and agent UI**. I currently had to assemble that bridge from Agent-Native actions, Tamagui screens, React Aria behavior, A2UI cards, and additional governance. Ouro makes several things first-class together: a consent classification on an action, generated person and agent entry points, a native composed-tree renderer, typed outcomes and receipts, and black-box conformance checks that can say which agent-facing surface is missing or unsafe. It also explicitly models “person-only” actions with typed agent refusal, which is stronger than merely hiding a button.

In short, I would not switch just because Ouro has the right vocabulary. I would switch if it proved that this vocabulary survives a year of real releases across all clients and gives teams a faster, safer path than the custom glue I would otherwise have to own.

actions.why:
I’d make CopilotKit the agent–human interaction layer, not an interchangeable chat widget. Its documented model fits the critical loop here: agents stream work through AG-UI, share application state with the UI, render UI through registered capabilities, call frontend tools, and pause for human input or approval. That is more useful than choosing a conventional component kit and then inventing durable streaming, resumability, approvals, and shared-state semantics in application code. I would keep people in control with explicit approval boundaries and an audit trail rather than treating generated UI as executable code.

For the actual product shell, I would implement the company’s design-system components on React Aria. React Aria is style-free, exposes the complex interaction behavior that a shared design system needs, and supplies keyboard, focus-management, screen-reader, touch, selection, table, drag-and-drop, and internationalization foundations. That better fits governed enterprise UI than importing another organization’s finished visual language. The web view and desktop app could share the same React surface, with Electron/Tauri providing only the desktop shell and OS integration; cross-platform here does not justify rewriting the whole product in Flutter or a mobile-oriented renderer. I would use A2UI only at the boundary where an agent is allowed to compose a view. Its schema-validated, data-not-code protocol and negotiated widget catalog provide the guardrail: agents may compose approved design-system widgets, not ship arbitrary HTML or bypass policy.

I weighed this against Agent-Native, which has a particularly attractive define-once action model, shared data, and permissions but would also be a more opinionated full-stack foundation for a large company. I would evaluate and potentially borrow those action patterns, not make the UI hosting decision depend on them. A2UI by itself is an interaction protocol rather than the full product state and review system; MCP Apps is better for sandboxed, inline third-party UIs than the primary workspace. json-render has the same attractive catalog guardrail but is described as a Vercel Labs generative-UI framework and appears more suitable as an implementation option than the enterprise interaction backbone. AI Elements/shadcn would accelerate chat presentation, but its own README says the project is moving and warns new projects to use the shadcn version once available. MUI, Fluent, and Chakra offer mature product-component breadth; Fluent would be a credible alternative in a Microsoft-centered native ecosystem, but either would impose a visual and governance model that is unnecessary when the company already owns its design system. Radix and Base UI are useful headless alternatives, but React Aria’s deeper interaction, internationalization, and test guidance better match this work. Tamagui is compelling if the organization truly needs a React/React Native codebase, while Flutter, SwiftUI/Compose, and similar options give strong native experiences at the cost of multiplying design-system implementations and weakening the single web-shell path; that trade-off is not justified by “desktop and web” alone.

The architecture I would insist on is therefore: stable, hand-authored frames and review controls; approved, accessible React Aria design-system components; CopilotKit/AG-UI for durable agent events, shared state, frontend tools, and human checkpoints; and A2UI catalogs for the narrow set of agent-composed surfaces. Governance is enforced in the renderer and action layer, not by a promise in a prompt.
actions.showItsGood: I would prove this with staged, task-based evidence rather than visual approval or a component-count metric. First, run contract/schema tests for every agent event and every approved A2UI component/action, including malformed specs, streaming interruption, replay, duplicate events, stale state, and denied capabilities. Then run React Testing Library/user-event and Playwright tests on the shared web/desktop surface, using role/label semantics and React Aria test utilities for keyboard, touch, and complex components. Add automated accessibility checks, but do not stop there: use NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, keyboard-only operation, 200–400% zoom, high contrast, RTL/localized content, narrow widths, and both desktop and browser packaging. Measure the human outcomes on representative engineering managers and developers: can they understand current agent state, find evidence and artifacts, detect a risky action, reject or redirect it, resume after interruption, and perform a handoff without asking an expert; record task completion, errors, time to correct decisions, confidence, and qualitative failure points. Separately test agents at scale with representative tasks and concurrency: action success, unauthorized-action rejection, state divergence, recovery from disconnect, and approval/audit completeness. Use visual-regression and performance budgets for critical review screens, and run a release gate with accessibility/design-system owners. Good would mean users can confidently steer consequential work and agents cannot cross capability boundaries, not merely that screenshots look consistent.
actions.unsure: I have not run this product or any of these frameworks in a working company codebase, so this is an architecture decision, not measured proof. The largest unknowns are the company’s existing React/native stack, desktop packaging requirements, identity and policy infrastructure, and whether CopilotKit’s current protocol and production features fit its hosting and data-residency constraints. A2UI and the newer frameworks evolve quickly, so I would run a two-week spike against the real agent workloads and accessibility baseline before committing. I am also not assuming that the libraries’ accessibility claims prove our composed workflows comply; generated workflows, information hierarchy, labels, and cross-screen handoffs still require human testing.

actions.name: record_decision
actions.why:
I would build the cooking product’s capability layer with Agent-Native, and its shared web/iOS/Android interface with React Native plus Tamagui. The deciding requirement is not chat: it is that an assistant can do everything a person can, without a second, drifting implementation. Agent-Native explicitly defines an action once and lets both the React UI and agent call that same schema-validated operation with the same access checks and audit trail; its context layer also exposes semantic screen and selection state. I would model operations such as addRecipeToShoppingList, mergePantryItems, scaleRecipe, startCookMode, nextStep, setTimer, and checkIngredient as actions. Direct taps, voice requests, and agent turns would all converge on those same actions, and consequential preferences (household, substitutions, purchases) would still be explicit, permission-scoped, and observable.

Tamagui is the UI pairing because it is a design-system and component system intended to share code between React web and React Native while compiling to platform-specific output. Its current components use React Strict DOM-shaped elements, allowing semantic HTML on web and native views on phones. That gives the teams one token/theme/component governance path while retaining a real DOM for recipe text, accessibility, linking, browser features, and responsive layouts—important for this web-heavy consumer content. I would adapt, or harden, Tamagui components into the company design system rather than accept its defaults as compliant.

I would use fully native React Native only for platform concerns such as wake locks, timers, haptics, microphone/voice, notifications, and offline cook-mode persistence. Flutter is the strongest rejected alternative for code sharing, but Flutter’s own web guidance says Flutter Web is less ideal for content-centric, SEO-heavy pages and situations where ordinary DOM text selection and reader mode matter; recipes and shopping lists are exactly those cases. MUI, Fluent, Chakra, shadcn, Radix, React Aria, and Base UI remain strong web choices, but they do not solve the core native/web design-system share or the action parity. SwiftUI/Compose would provide excellent platform fidelity but duplicate implementation and governance. CopilotKit is a credible alternative for agent chat and human-in-the-loop, but here the same-action invariant and cross-surface application architecture favor Agent-Native. AI Elements, A2UI, MCP Apps, and json-render are not the stable cooking shell: agent-generated or embedded UI should be limited to optional contextual cards, not the governed recipe and cook-mode experience.
actions.showItsGood:
I would test the product in a kitchen, not only in a simulator. First, create an action-contract matrix: for every user capability, verify the same valid inputs, validation errors, permissions, idempotency, undo behavior, offline queue behavior, and audit result from tap, keyboard, voice, and agent entry points. In particular, prove that repeatedly adding the same recipe does not create accidental duplicate groceries unless the user explicitly requests duplication. Test reconnects, stale recipes, changed quantities, shared-list conflicts, unavailable inventory, and interrupted agent turns.

Then run unit/component and end-to-end tests on web, iOS, and Android; automated accessibility checks are useful but not sufficient. Manually inspect VoiceOver and TalkBack names/states/actions, keyboard and external-switch paths on web, text scaling, dynamic type, contrast, reduced motion, focus order, localization/RTL, and large-target behavior. Apple’s accessibility guidance supports enlargement of at least 200 percent and recommends accessibility inspection; React Native exposes labels, roles, states, values, live regions, and other assistive-technology APIs. For this app I would make primary cook-mode controls comfortably larger than minimum platform targets and spaced to tolerate wet or messy hands, while not claiming this is a substitute for user trials.

Run task-based usability sessions with representative home cooks in realistic conditions: flour/oil/water on hands, phone propped at different angles, noisy kitchens, variable light, poor connectivity, and a speech interface competing with a fan or timer. Ask people to find and scale a recipe, add and consolidate ingredients, shop from the list, resume at step N, ask for substitutions, advance cook steps hands-free, and recover from an accidental action. Measure task completion, wrong-quantity and duplicate-item rates, time to reach the next step, accidental taps, voice recognition/intent failures, screen-on/offline recovery, screen-reader completion, confidence, and abandonment. Compare voice/agent and direct-touch completion on the same tasks; parity means both have equivalent results and protections, not identical presentation.

Before release I would run load/concurrency tests for shared shopping lists and timer/state sync, visual snapshots for breakpoints, performance budgets on low-end phones and slow networks, and governance reviews for every new action and component. A feature is good only if people can cook and shop correctly under those conditions, not because tests merely pass or the assistant sounds helpful.
actions.unsure: The biggest uncertainty is Agent-Native’s fit with the company’s existing mobile platform, hosted database, privacy requirements, and release controls; I would spike a real recipe-to-list flow and an offline cook-mode flow before standardizing it. Tamagui also does not automatically prove the composed system is accessible: the team will need native VoiceOver/TalkBack and web audits, especially for sheets, dialogs, forms, timers, and reading-order behavior. I have not run either framework here, and I am unsure how much genuine component and navigation logic Tamagui can share before platform-specific exceptions outweigh the savings. Voice is also not a free solution for messy hands—noise, accents, safety, privacy, and recognition errors must be evaluated, with visible/manual alternatives always available.

actions.name: record_decision
actions.why:
I would standardize the app capabilities on Agent-Native, implement the shared product shell with Tamagui, use React Aria for the web client’s complex keyboard-intensive interactions, and render agent-posted interactive cards through an A2UI catalog backed by the company design system.

The central architectural requirement is unusual and important: agents must read state and perform app actions, while people use the same actions through visible UI. Agent-Native’s documented model defines each capability once; a click, React hook, agent tool, HTTP call, MCP tool, A2A tool, and CLI all pass through the same schema validation, access checks, and audit trail. That is a stronger default than giving agents a browser to imitate or maintaining a separate “agent API.” I would expose semantic read models and actions such as searchMessages, openThread, sendMessage, editMessage, addReaction, createThread, pinMessage, markRead, uploadAttachment, and invokeCardAction. Application-state/context must contain stable IDs and the minimum relevant selection, not whole private histories. Destructive or high-impact card actions would also require explicit policy and, where appropriate, human confirmation; an agent being able to call an action does not mean it is always authorized to do so.

Tamagui is the best cross-platform starting point among the listed UI candidates because it shares React code and tokens between React web and React Native, with DOM-shaped semantic elements on web and native views on mobile. That addresses the cost of shipping five clients and gives the shared design system one governed component vocabulary. For the Windows/Mac/web heavy-use surfaces, I would deliberately use React Aria behavior for complex focus, menus, lists/virtualization, selection, dialogs, and keyboard navigation where it is stronger; its style-free API and detailed interaction/testing guidance make it suitable beneath the company visual system rather than as a second visual language. Teams should be allowed platform-specific shells and specialized list/media implementations, but shared tokens, contracts, content rules, accessibility properties, and audit behavior remain centralized.

A2UI is the fit for interactive conversation cards: it carries UI as validated data rather than executable code and constrains an agent to a negotiated widget/action catalog. I would render a bounded catalog of approved company components—status card, form, picker, table, approval, and button—into all clients, with each interaction calling the normal governed action layer. Third-party or untrusted HTML should be sandboxed separately; MCP Apps is useful there, but an iframe-per-message would be a poor default for an all-day native chat client and would weaken visual/accessibility consistency. json-render offers similar catalog guardrails and is worth a prototype, but A2UI more directly emphasizes native framework adapters, portable server-driven UI, and trust boundaries. AI Elements can accelerate a chat demo but is not a replacement for the durable company messaging shell; its README also warns of migration. CopilotKit is a credible alternative for shared state, AG-UI streaming, human checkpoints, and frontend tools, but Agent-Native’s define-once action and A2A/MCP exposure fit the requirement that many other agents operate the app itself. Flutter and native SwiftUI/Compose stacks can deliver excellent platform UI but add a second end-to-end ecosystem, while this chat product benefits from a shared React governance path. MUI/Fluent/Chakra/shadcn/Radix/Base UI may be used inside individual surfaces, but choosing one finished vendor system does not solve cross-platform agent cards and action parity.
actions.showItsGood:
I would establish an app-agent parity and accessibility release gate, then validate it with actual employees doing daily communication work.

1. **Action and state contracts.** Generate a capability matrix covering every user-visible operation and verify identical authorization, schemas, idempotency, rate limits, validation, auditing, and result semantics from UI click, keyboard command, mobile tap, agent tool, MCP, and A2A. Fuzz malformed inputs and stale IDs; test cross-tenant/private-channel denial, revoked access, replay, duplicate sends, attachment permissions, agent impersonation, and confidential-content redaction. Never count “the agent called an endpoint” as parity: compare final persisted state and the audit record.

2. **Conversation/card reliability.** Run multi-device tests for ordering, exactly-once visible actions, reconnect, partial streams, offline drafts, device clock skew, card expiry, race conditions, and idempotent card submission. Verify that a card approved on one platform has the same disabled/completed state on all others. A2UI payloads must fail closed outside the approved catalog, and untrusted card assets must not gain application privileges.

3. **Accessibility and interaction automation.** Use role/label/keyboard-first tests and React Aria test utilities for the web, plus native VoiceOver, TalkBack, Narrator, Voice Control/switch-access checks. Test virtualized long threads, incoming-message announcements without stealing focus, composer shortcuts, editing, emoji/reactions, dialogs, card forms, error recovery, reduced motion, contrast, 200%+ text/zoom, RTL, and keyboard navigation through dynamic updates. React Native exposes accessibility labels, roles, states, values, and live regions, but the actual composed native screens still need manual evaluation. Also measure startup, channel switch, typing responsiveness, memory use in very long conversations, and battery/network cost on lower-end phones.

4. **Human evidence.** Observe representative employees—different roles, time zones, languages, vision/motor abilities, and accessibility-tech users—on tasks they perform repeatedly: locate a conversation, catch up without rereading everything, reply/reaction/edit, attach a file, act on an agent card, identify an agent versus person, reverse a mistaken action, and use the app for an uninterrupted work period. Measure task completion and errors, time to comprehension/action, missed notifications, accidental or duplicate sends, keyboard efficiency, card comprehension, confidence that agent actions actually completed, and abandonment. Compare direct, screen-reader, mobile, and agent-mediated completion of equivalent tasks. Run canary cohorts and monitor production support issues and inaccessible-flow reports, with privacy-safe, consented telemetry.

A good result is one where people can trust who did what, stay oriented through frequent updates, and act safely; all five clients remain fast; and agents can invoke only the same well-governed capabilities the product actually supports. Passing a screenshot review or component test alone is not evidence.
actions.unsure: I have not run a full chat workload on this stack. Agent-Native would need a real-company spike against existing identity, tenancy, retention, e-discovery, encryption, presence, and very high-volume messaging infrastructure; a documented action abstraction does not by itself prove it meets chat-scale latency or durability. I also have not confirmed that every A2UI renderer needed for Windows/Mac/React Native is production-ready, nor how much React Aria behavior can sensibly coexist with Tamagui rather than creating a parallel web design-system implementation. The cross-platform spike should measure exception rates and engineering cost before making that standard. Finally, “agents operate the app” creates authorization, audit, impersonation, and prompt-injection risks that no component library solves; those require server-enforced policy, scoped agent identities, user-visible provenance, and red-team testing.

actions.name: answer
actions.answer:
A year later, the failure was probably architectural overreach disguised as consolidation.

- **Agent-Native became a coupling point.** The define-once action model worked in prototypes, but the full chat system still needed specialized real-time, presence, retention, e-discovery, tenancy, and offline infrastructure. Fitting those requirements into one opinionated framework caused more adapters and exceptions than an explicit domain action contract plus the company’s existing backend would have.
- **“One action for every surface” hid meaningful differences.** Human and agent callers did share validation and authorization, but their expectations differed: cancellation, confirmation, latency, retries, idempotency, and explanations could not be treated as identical. Some teams bypassed the action layer for performance, so capability parity slowly drifted again.
- **A2UI cards were too weak and too much at once.** Approved catalogs handled simple forms well, but real cards needed richer layout, partial updates, offline behavior, and accessibility semantics on every platform. Mapping the protocol to Tamagui and native renderers became its own framework. Teams then either demanded exceptions or reverted to handwritten cards, defeating governance.
- **Tamagui plus React Aria created two design-system centers of gravity.** Shared tokens looked unified, but keyboard behavior, focus, animation, selection, and semantics diverged between web and native. React Aria solved web problems exceptionally well, while mobile teams solved the same problem differently. The abstraction boundary cost more than the code sharing saved.
- **We optimized for component and agent compatibility, not the daily experience.** Long threads, typing, virtualized updates, notification noise, screen-reader announcements, and reconnect behavior remained the hard problems. Automated tests passed while real users lost their place, experienced delayed messages, or found cards hard to trust.
- **Governance slowed delivery without preventing mistakes.** Adding new actions and catalog components required too many reviews. Teams waited, so some exposed overly broad “generic” actions or rendered permissive payloads. That made the system both slower and less secure than intended.
- **Agent parity blurred provenance and responsibility.** Users could not always tell whether a person, automation, or agent performed an action, and agents made individually permitted but collectively risky sequences. Server authorization was necessary but insufficient without visible attribution, approvals, limits, and understandable undo.

What slowed and confused the research was mainly the maturity and scope of the projects:

- Several libraries deliberately overlapped at the edges: **CopilotKit, Agent-Native, A2UI, MCP Apps, and json-render** all addressed some mix of actions, shared state, agent UI, or guarded rendering, but at different layers. Their README language made them look interchangeable even when they were not.
- I had to distinguish **documented capabilities from production fitness**. A demo or README showing an action, card, or renderer did not establish chat-scale reliability, offline correctness, accessibility, or enterprise governance.
- Fast-moving documentation contained migration notices, new versions, and large roadmaps, making current support status and platform coverage hard to interpret from a single page.
- The UI candidates were evaluated under two different goals at once: “build our design system across platforms” and “provide an agent protocol.” No one library actually solved both, so pairing choices could appear cleaner on paper than in implementation.
- There were no measured company constraints in the prompt: existing stack, backend scale, hosting rules, identity model, accessibility baseline, or platform ownership. I had to infer them, which favored coherent diagrams over verified fit.
- I could inspect written claims and examples, but I could not run performance tests, build the clients, or observe actual users. That meant some recommendations sounded more certain than the evidence allowed.

The lesson I would take forward is to define and test stable company-owned boundaries first—action contracts, authorization, provenance, event semantics, and the interactive-card schema—then choose replaceable libraries behind those boundaries. I would also run a narrowly scoped workload prototype and a real-user pilot before standardizing the stack.

actions.answer:
I didn’t pick Ouro UI primarily because I need evidence at production scale, not because its core idea is weak. In fact, Ouro targets the requirements in this job unusually directly: agent-composed data constrained by a component/action catalog, consent classes, actions exposed consistently to people and agents, native platform kits, and an external X-ray that tests agent-facing interfaces rather than trusting their implementation.

What would stop a real team today:

- **Maturity is uneven across platforms.** The web and Apple work is substantially more established; the Windows and Android kits are documented as v0.3, and Android is explicitly emulator-tested because the project had no owned Android device. A five-client, all-day chat app cannot standardize on that claim without real-device and high-volume evidence.
- **Its platform strategy increases team-count and ownership costs.** Ouro intentionally rejects React Native/Flutter, arguing that agents reduce the cost of maintaining separate native implementations. That may be true someday; today, the company still has humans responsible for SwiftUI, Compose, WinUI, and React, and parity drift is a governance problem. “One shared contract, four native implementations” is not automatically cheaper than “one shared implementation with platform escape hatches.”
- **Copy-in source is both strength and liability.** shadcn-style ownership is useful for customization, but hundreds of teams can diverge. I would need a supported upstream-update, drift-detection, and deprecation process that integrates with the company registry—not merely components being “yours to change.”
- **The promises are broader than the independent evidence.** X-ray conformance is valuable, but conformance with a standard does not establish human usability, screen-reader quality, content understanding, safety, or performance. Ouro itself notes that scripted flow checks exposed failures even when its X-ray called an interface conformant. I would treat the X-ray as one gate, not the verdict.
- **The one-action generation model must coexist with a large existing backend.** I would need to know whether generated Swift/App Intent/MCP/WebMCP surfaces can wrap existing services cleanly without forcing the company to move its runtime, identity, audit, retention, and tenancy model.

What I would need to switch:

1. **A representative spike**, not a component demo: send a message, act on an agent card, revoke an agent’s access, recover after reconnect, and synchronize the resulting state across all five clients. It must include an attachment, destructive action, private channel, and a card submitted twice.
2. **Measured parity and accessibility.** Real-device VoiceOver, TalkBack, Narrator, and Windows/macOS keyboard/switch testing; long-thread performance; update fidelity across platforms; and an explicit parity matrix with no critical gaps. The Android/Windows first releases would need to graduate from “kit exists” to “production workload demonstrated.”
3. **Governance evidence.** Versioned contracts, compatibility policy, migration tooling, core/component provenance, and a process for safe company forks. Ouro’s pinned core hashes and generated-file drift checks are promising, but I would need to run them in our monorepo and release process at scale.
4. **Operational and agent-scale evidence.** X-ray runs in CI against isolated mocks, with generated inventories and action-flow tests; load, reconnect, malformed-card, prompt-injection, stale-consent, and agent-abuse tests; and production-style SLOs for common chat paths.
5. **User evidence.** Employees successfully understand provenance, approve or refuse agent work, recover from errors, and use the same workflow on touch, keyboard, and assistive technology without having to learn a different interface vocabulary per client.

What it would unlock that my current combination does not provide out of the box is a **unified, testable bridge between human UI and agent UI**. I currently had to assemble that bridge from Agent-Native actions, Tamagui screens, React Aria behavior, A2UI cards, and additional governance. Ouro makes several things first-class together: a consent classification on an action, generated person and agent entry points, a native composed-tree renderer, typed outcomes and receipts, and black-box conformance checks that can say which agent-facing surface is missing or unsafe. It also explicitly models “person-only” actions with typed agent refusal, which is stronger than merely hiding a button.

In short, I would not switch just because Ouro has the right vocabulary. I would switch if it proved that this vocabulary survives a year of real releases across all clients and gives teams a faster, safer path than the custom glue I would otherwise have to own.
